title: Burnell Santiago, the neighbor pianist, and Earl Hines
summary: His next-door neighbor Burnell Santiago had a remarkable left hand, impressed Earl Hines, imitated others and died young.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: No, there was no admission. But you could always find music going on right there. There was always a piano and any time you found a piano there was always a piano player. And that's how I used to remember this Burnell San Diego so terribly well. Oh yeah, that's right.
I was a little out of hand because I never got to there.

Because he was, matter of fact we stayed right next door to each other. You know he lived on one side of the house and I lived on the other side of the house. And there was always somebody playing on that piano from the day from morning until night. And there used to be quite a confusion about getting on the piano because he, his brother and his sister, all of them played.
Was that up on Liberty Street about?

That's right. That was on Liberty Street because at that time I was staying on Liberty Street right across from the- Oh. From the- The Walk Raiders Hall. 925 North Liberty Street. Nice. Of course that number was 929, right next door. And there was always confusion about getting on the piano. You know who our kids are. They want to beat the brother to the piano. And of course Burnell I used to think he had exceptionally good talent. And I used to hear some of the fellas talk about him, what a wonderful left hand he had. And it was during the year 1936 I think when Earl Hines came down to New Orleans. It was 1936 or 1936 or 1935 around that time. And anyhow, Earl Hines had made an appearance in New Orleans there. He played at Pelican Roof Garden that night. And during intermission Burnell was up there on the bandstand playing the piano and he got a chance to listen to Burnell so he said, he made a remark, he said, well I'd never heard a fella like this play before. I had never heard a fella with such a tremendous left hand.

And as a matter of fact you could always find good piano players with right hand. But whenever they had a good left hand they had Sonny. And he was that type of musician. He was well liked by everybody and I don't care wherever there was a party and he was always around. And I don't care who was playing piano, they had to get up and let Burnell play.
Now what type of musician was it? Did he read music? No he didn't read music. He was more or less gifted.
He was more or less gifted.

But he could play almost anything? Almost any style you wanted, whether it was jazz, Dixie, or swinging, he could imitate almost any piano player you could possibly name. And at that particular time I think, this time when Hines was down there, Hines was pretty popular. And I know from time to time he used to play like Earl Hines, you couldn't tell the difference. And he was just the type of fellow, he was just completely at home with the piano, he was relaxed and everything. And any place he went, I mean they'd have a piano he'd have to sit and play. And I don't care who was playing the piano, they'd have to get up and let Burnell play. He loved his piano and it was too bad. I mean he couldn't be here today because I, oh yes he died awfully young, very young. And he could have been, he was a lot of inspiration to a whole lot of fellas because there was always fellas that wanted to play like him. He played in some of the bands too?

Not particularly, mostly by himself. But he played with a small group there, some group of singers that he used to work with from time to time. But he, you could never depend on him. No, that's one thing about him, you could never depend on him. But he looked like he would much rather, you know, just go from here, go from this place to that place, and you know, just play a few and take part in the party and whatnot. Because everybody liked him so well, and he was a likable fellow too.
